name: Igniting Karachi - Five minutes at a time!

content.title: Igniting Karachi - Five minutes at a time!
content.summary: Ignite Karachi, a timed talk series, is organised by the Critical Creative Innovative Thinking (CCIT) and is intended to light a spark in the audience to think differently.

media.alt: Igniting Karachi - Five minutes at a time!
Igniting Karachi - Five minutes at a time!

content.text: ''May my words ignite a spark in all to always think creatively and outside the box...,"commented Nafeesa Jalal, a public health consultant, during her five minutes at the third edition of the Ignite Karachi series held at Aga Khan University today. Ignite Karachi, a timed talk series, is organised by the Critical Creative Innovative Thinking (CCIT) group and is intended to light a spark in the audience to think differently.

Presenters have no more than five minutes and exactly 20 slides to share what is on their mind. This fast-paced, succinct format makes the event as much of a challenge for the speakers as entertaining for the audience. Presenters can choose any topic as long as it falls under the broad categories of healthcare, biomedicine or social good.

Today's session saw a number of different issues being addressed ranging from maternal mortality and efforts being made in South Africa to reduce its incidence to the importance of clear communication in health care to journeys of self-discovery in the wake of disaster.

For Drs Taha Sabri and Nuzhat Faruqi, the spark to make a difference was lit in the wake of two very distinct tragedies, the 2013 Abbas Town bombing and the 2010 floods respectively. For Dr Sabri, it meant the setting up of the Humanity Initiative, an organisation with the goal of helping people in dire need, and in the process gaining a sense of contentment. While for Dr Faruqi her work throughout the country led to the discovery of the great scenic wealth of Pakistan. Dr Faruqi now advocates serving humanity and discovering the natural beauty of the country in tandem.

Huma Baqir, a third year medical student at AKU, was of the view that good communication and empathy are essential qualities of a physician and needed to break the barriers of being perceived as mere classroom-taught phenomenon.

Using stories, animations, poems and even tag games, according to Mayera Tufail, a second year medical student at AKU, were some of the innovative ways with which teaching complex biochemical pathways and anatomical structures could be made more interesting.

Perhaps the most inspiring presentation, one that offered hope to many who know of someone suffering from age-related brain disease, was that of Rehan Rehman, a faculty member at Nixor College. His contention that an ageing brain is adaptive and compensates for age-related loss in cognition could lead to positive implications for those suffering from diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.
Other presenters included Hassan Bin Fahim, Mayank Aranke, Mohammad Taha Anver and Nick Brown.

Ignite Karachi 3 showcased an interesting series of presentations that were short enough to match the concentration span of the average listener yet long enough to leave the audience thinking about issues affecting our world. CCIT hopes to hold more Ignite events in future, with an ever increasing diversity of speakers and topics.
Written by Huma Baqir (year 3) and Kanwal Nayani (year 5), medical students at the Aga Khan University's Medical College in Karachi.
